Maternity UIF claims

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How easy is it to claim your Maternity UIF benefits?

Unique Selling Point:
The Department of Labour is struggling to keep up with UIF payments and many people are outraged because they are either not paid out, or they have to wait long for their payment. In addition, there are countless stories of paperwork getting lost and general inefficiencies within the Department. We speak to a group of women who have been trying for months to get what is due to them paid out.

Along came UIF Assist centres, private businesses that were supposed to make life easier for the claimants. This meant that, in the case of pregnant mothers, women could pay a once-off fee and their claims would be processed hassle free. However, some of these companies could not deliver on their promises.

Summary:
Giving birth is a financially stressful time in any woman's life. Many women do not get paid their full salary during their maternity leave and they rely on Maternity UIF payments to get them through this time. Suddenly there's an extra mouth to feed in the house and a string of unexpected expenses. By law a woman can claim Maternity UIF if she has been contributing to the fund. But this is a huge source of frustration for new moms. Many approach the Department of Labour themselves, only to be sent back because they have the wrong, or incomplete forms. Then they are told to wait 4-6 weeks. After that, they contact the Department asking for their first payment, only to discover the the DOL has lost a form, or an entire file and they need to start the process all over again. In most cases women only get paid out (if at all) once they are back at work. And that completely defeats the purpose of the Maternity UIF, since it is meant to alleviate financial pressure during maternity leave.

Because of this struggle there are a host of UIF assist companies that assist mothers, but they too are struggling and in many cases fail to deliver on their promises. They simply take their fee and run. Companies like Moms Assist ask a fee of around R750, and for that they will submit your paperwork, stand in the queue on your behalf - basically make the whole process hassle free. However, companies struggle to deliver on their promises because of the chaos at the Department of Labour.

We will speak to the Department about the problems the Department is experiencing as well as the private agencies, and whether or not they are being regulated to some extent.

Further information:
It seems that since about 2012, the Department's system has been changed, resulting in massive backlogs and mistakes in loading and processing claims. While many people eventually get paid out, it seems to average about 9 months after they return to work, which means that during the first months of their babies’ lives, they have to go into debt and undergo the stress of running around submitting and resbumitting forms. Most of the women who have contacted us are middle class and so can probably find a way to survive, although many of them have to cut their maternity leave short, but imagine all the domestic workers or other low-paid employees and single mothers who are utterly dependent on this money. Also,
UIF seems to be a huge problem across the board, but the maternity benefits are an easy way to tell the story with an emotional face!

The other element is the numerous agencies that claim to assist mothers in submitting and processing their claims, take an upfront payment (usually between R500 and R700) and then do nothing whatsoever to help. It’s not their fault if the Department can’t process documents, but surely if they know the situation, they are essentially offering a service and collecting fees under false pretences. Some of them seem to have closed down and reopened under another name.

1. Stats from the Department of Labour (2015 is the most recent available) show that 93,879 Maternity UIF applications were made country-wide and they claim that 90,581 were paid out. At the same time the DOL also reported around 72,000 queries and compaints - this is obviously not just for Maternity UIF, but there is definitly something wrong. I have attached a spreadsheet with details.

2. Case Study 1: Aabida Khan - Teacher from Lenasia - She has been stuggling to get a payout since March 2017. Her baby was born in January. Her husband was unemployed at the time so it all put a huge financial stress on the family. She has phoned the department more than 20 times. re-submitted various documents and now they are simply saying they can’t find her on the system. She is obviously very frustrated.

Case Study 2: Lerato (Not sure of surname yet) - low-level office worker from Klerksdorp. She applied in January 2017. Baby was born in January. The department lost her forms no less than 5 times. She had to resubmit to various sub-departments within the DOL. Eventually case was escalated to Mafikeng and still some documents went missing. She is not married and the father of the baby is unemployed. She had no income from January to May. Her mother had to help. Very dire financial situation. We can film interview with her and her mother in Schweizer Reineke. The mother is now looking after the baby as she went back to work in June. She speaks well and describes her levels of frustration clearly. She did get paid out eventually after 7 months, when she started writing to heads of departments at DOL.

Case Study 3: Claire Hollick - Upper class - Johannesburg. She applied through an Agency and after a while the Agency just dissappeared and she has been left with nothing. She speaks of financial discomfort and had to extend her credit card.

Press Release:


Maternity UIF
Maternity UIF payments are often the only source of income new mothers receive in their first few months
with a new baby. But it seems the Department of Labour has been falling behind in these pay-outs and
hundreds of desperate women aren’t receiving payments due to them. Carte Blanche investigates.

Script:


Maternity UIF

The first cry of a baby is a magical moment for a mother. Her life has changed. But with the precious joy comes responsibility....
Link
From the moment the baby is born the new mother has to juggle between two tasks – caring for her child and shouldering the financial burden that comes with new life.
V/o
Mmapule fell pregnant over 2 years ago and knew from the start that she would need to rely on Maternity UIF to get her through the 3 months she was unable to work.
Mmapule
It was basically going to help me with buying formula for my child and even the pampers.

She started the process of claiming UIF in September 2015 just after her little boy was born.
Mmapule
You know with the Department of Labour in Soshanguve everytime I went there it was like story after the other. They would tell me no we've mixed your documents with this other person's document so now we can not make a pay out. Come back after three weeks. Then I went there after three weeks. Then they'll say you know what just leave your papers here, we'll call you con Monday. It's been a period of two years now, running the same procedure.
V/o
Not having access to her Maternity UIF, life as a single mother was very hard for Mmapule.
Mmapule
I wasn't getting money from anyone. It was either my sister who used to put a hand in or my mom.
Link
It's not hard to find women with a similar story. Mothers from all walks of life are struggling to get their maternity UIF payment from the Department of Labour.
V/o
Lerato delivered her baby at the end of April and soon afterwards she started the process of claiming her Maternity UIF.
Lerato
I get there and they explain to me that you literally need to get UI19 forms from every employer I have had for the last 4 years.
V/o
This is the first obstacle most women are faced with. The Department of Labour needs complete employment details for the 4 years preceding the maternity claim.

With UI19 forms from all four of her previous employers, and her newborn in tow, Lerato went back to the UIF office the following week.
Lerato
I'm now assisted by a new gentleman standing at this first point of contact who is like no you need U19 forms plus a certificate of service. So then I'm like, breathe in breathe out... I'm like couldn't they have told me this last time.
V/o
The next Friday she was told she needed a salary schedule, and once she produced this document she was told it was on an incorrect template...
Lerato
Everytime you deal with somebody they have a new instruction on what I must do. The person you spoke to the day before didn't give you the same instruction. So, everyday I get a new hula hoop that I must jump through to get through to that station or that person.
V/o
Makhosonke Buthelezi, the Director of Communication and Marketing at the
Unemployment Insurance Fund says they successfully process around 100,000 maternity UIF claims annually.
Makonsonke Buthelezi
One of the biggest challenges that we face is the incomplete information on the form. You find that the claimant submits the form and when you go through it you realize that there is outstanding information.
Link
Complaints about the Department range from rude call centre staff, to lost documents and paperwork. The mothers that we spoke to are very frustrated with the service provided.
Makhosonke
I think most of the cases where documents get lost is when there is still outstanding information.

How can you lose documents that have been scanned?

Systematically it does happen sometimes. – as it happens with your normal computer if it shuts down – some tend to get missing in the process.
V/o
Disillusioned by the service she received, Lerato decided to try ufiling – the Department's online UIF claiming system.
Lerato
The system online is like extremely slow but I'm like okay, I can handle that, I can stomach that. But midway through the process it asks me to confirm which Lerato I am. An as I'm about to click on the Lerato that I am the whole system just timed out.

And then when I refreshed there's this big sign on the thing that says I'd been blocked out of the system
Makonsonke Buthelezi
Ufiling is very reliable, however we've experienced lately some technical glitches and we've got a little bit of a backlog on Ufiling. But we have reconfigured our personnel to go and assist in terms of trying to clear the backlog.

At the moment Ufiling is not mobile friendly, but the Department is in the process of developing an App to make it easy to submit claims via cellphone.
Claire
What would you say is at the heart of the issues that are being experienced by the Department of Labour when it comes to UIF?
Makonsonke Buthelezi
From our side it's compliance, compliance, compliance. Employers must really try submit, declare their employees tot he UIF regularly.
Stephanie
I've seen it a lot. Employers are not compliant. They deduct the UIF, they pay it over and they think my job is done.
V/o
Stephanie runs her own UIF consultancy and feels the Department should not be judged so harshly. She says many employers fail to declare their employees on a monthly basis leading to incorrect information and employment history gaps on the Department's systems.
Stephanie
It is a multi million financial institution , so yea, of course they are afraid of fraud and therefore documents need to be 100% correctly completed. And when it comes to HR they don't always know how to complete the documents. There's a certain way of completing the documents and making sure it is correct. Checking that the registered address with UIF is the one that you're still at. Because that's all verification on the UI19.
V/o
The Department also says that the entire UIF system is in the process of getting a makeover. Additional staff are being trained for call centres, systems are being streamlined and UIF centres will soon have free wifi for customers.
Makhosonke
I know in the background there is work that is happening to realize some of the elements of the service action delivery plan. Within 6 months, I would like to invite you and we can assess the situation.
Claire
That's June 2018
Makhosonke
Correct.

In the meantime it has been over six months since Lerato submitted her claim and she has made no real headway in getting her UIF payout. She is depserate.
Lerato
I am in a panic state because I am like what happens to all the things I must finance with this money? I can't go back to my daughter's school and say sorry UIF hasn't paid me...
V/o
Mmapule had no choice but to make ends meet, but the R3,000 she was fighting for would have made a world of difference...
Mmapule
I would have got like the nappies and I would also get right medication for my child and I would also get the right formula, because not that whenever you're not getting any pay you will just go for a lesser formula And sometimes it affects the health of the baby.




PROMO 1 10”
Women from all walks of life are struggling to claim their Maternity UIF from the Department of Labour. Why is it so difficult to get what is rightfully owed to you?


PROMO 2 15”


Without Maternity UIF, many women are battling to make ends meet.

I wasn't getting money from anyone. It was either my sister who used to put a hand in or my mom.

Is the Department failing new mothers?


PROMO 3 15”
The Department of Labour has a very bad reputation when it comes to Maternity UIF payments.

Everytime you deal with somebody they have a new instruction on what I must do.

But what sits at the heart of the Maternity UIF problem?

And that completely defeats the purpose of the Maternity UIF, since it is meant to alleviate financial pressure during maternity leave. Because of this struggle there are a host of UIF assist companies that assist mothers, but they too are struggling and in many cases fail to deliver on their promises. They simply take their fee and run. Companies like Moms Assist ask a fee of around R750, and for that they will submit your paperwork, stand in the queue on your behalf - basically make the whole process hassle free. However, companies struggle to deliver on their promises because of the chaos at the Department of Labour. We will speak to the Department about the problems the Department is experiencing as well as the private agencies, and whether or not they are being regulated to some extent.
metadata.Further information: It seems that since about 2012, the Department's system has been changed, resulting in massive backlogs and mistakes in loading and processing claims. While many people eventually get paid out, it seems to average about 9 months after they return to work, which means that during the first months of their babies’ lives, they have to go into debt and undergo the stress of running around submitting and resbumitting forms. Most of the women who have contacted us are middle class and so can probably find a way to survive, although many of them have to cut their maternity leave short, but imagine all the domestic workers or other low-paid employees and single mothers who are utterly dependent on this money. Also, UIF seems to be a huge problem across the board, but the maternity benefits are an easy way to tell the story with an emotional face! The other element is the numerous agencies that claim to assist mothers in submitting and processing their claims, take an upfront payment (usually between R500 and R700) and then do nothing whatsoever to help. It’s not their fault if the Department can’t process documents, but surely if they know the situation, they are essentially offering a service and collecting fees under false pretences. Some of them seem to have closed down and reopened under another name. 1. Stats from the Department of Labour (2015 is the most recent available) show that 93,879 Maternity UIF applications were made country-wide and they claim that 90,581 were paid out. At the same time the DOL also reported around 72,000 queries and compaints - this is obviously not just for Maternity UIF, but there is definitly something wrong. I have attached a spreadsheet with details. 2. Case Study 1: Aabida Khan - Teacher from Lenasia - She has been stuggling to get a payout since March 2017. Her baby was born in January. Her husband was unemployed at the time so it all put a huge financial stress on the family. She has phoned the department more than 20 times. re-submitted various documents and now they are simply saying they can’t find her on the system. She is obviously very frustrated. Case Study 2: Lerato (Not sure of surname yet) - low-level office worker from Klerksdorp. She applied in January 2017. Baby was born in January. The department lost her forms no less than 5 times. She had to resubmit to various sub-departments within the DOL. Eventually case was escalated to Mafikeng and still some documents went missing. She is not married and the father of the baby is unemployed. She had no income from January to May. Her mother had to help. Very dire financial situation. We can film interview with her and her mother in Schweizer Reineke. The mother is now looking after the baby as she went back to work in June. She speaks well and describes her levels of frustration clearly. She did get paid out eventually after 7 months, when she started writing to heads of departments at DOL. Case Study 3: Claire Hollick - Upper class - Johannesburg. She applied through an Agency and after a while the Agency just dissappeared and she has been left with nothing. She speaks of financial discomfort and had to extend her credit card.
